items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence has entered animation classrooms faster than research has been able to describe what it does to learning. This study developed a “Learning-Thinking-Applying-Creating” (LTAC) integrated teaching model built on an open-source AIGC toolchain and evaluated it in a twelve-week quasi-experiment with second-year animation students, two intact classes being allocated to an experimental or a control condition. Cognitive load was measured with a three-subscale instrument adapted from Paas and from Leppink and colleagues, and divergent thinking with an abbreviated Torrance-type battery scored for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration by two trained raters who worked blind to group and occasion (intraclass correlations 0.86 to 0.91). Data were collected at pretest, mid-test, and posttest. Analysis of covariance indicated that the intervention lowered extraneous load and raised germane load while leaving intrinsic load unchanged. Repeated-measures analysis revealed selective gains: originality and elaboration improved more in the experimental group, whereas fluency and flexibility rose in both. Structural equation modelling was consistent with a differentiated mechanism, in which lower extraneous load predicted fluency and flexibility, germane load related to originality and elaboration indirectly through a deep-processing strategy, and intrinsic load showed an inverted-U association with the creative-thinking composite. Because the outcome measure is domain-general, the results speak to divergent thinking rather than to animation ability as such. The study extends cognitive load theory into generative-AI-supported creative education and offers animation programmes a reproducible instructional design that lowers production barriers while protecting deep creative work.

analysis.methods: Two theoretical anchors shape the model. The revised Bloom taxonomy supplies an ordered ladder of cognitive objectives, while constructivist learning theory insists that knowledge is assembled by the learner rather than transmitted intact. Read together, they yield four sequenced stages, each pinned to a rising rung of the taxonomy and each equipped with a distinct AIGC entry point. The Learning stage handles knowledge input. Micro-lecture videos and interactive animations, generated with AIGC support, deliver foundational concepts in a form that keeps early extraneous demands low 38 . Comparable media designs in art and design programmes-augmented-reality frameworks for practice-based education 39 and animation-based problem-solving materials 40 -indicate that the delivery format itself carries part of the instructional burden. Instructor-student interaction here stays largely one-directional, and the output is judged by a recall-and-comprehension rubric. The Thinking stage lifts the target objective toward analysis: AI-driven problem scenarios prompt learners to interrogate what they have absorbed, forcing conceptual reconstruction rather than passive acceptance 1 . Assessment shifts to the quality of reasoning traces students leave behind. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 In the Applying stage, skill transfer takes over. Students turn to open-source animation software to realize concrete schemes, moving from understanding to execution 3 . The teacher's role becomes that of a troubleshooter, and deliverables are scored against technical fidelity and completion. The Creating stage sits at the apex of the ladder, where an AIGC co-creation platform hosts original animation projects 10 . Here human-machine collaboration is genuinely reciprocal, and originality, coherence, and expressive intent form the evaluation criteria. Figure 2 traces the full activity sequence and tool-embedding nodes across the four stages. The escalation across stages is deliberate rather than incidental. Learning targets recall and comprehension; Thinking moves to analysis; Applying demands transfer into production; and Creating asks for synthesis and original expression. Each stage also hands something forward, since the artefact and the competence produced at one stage become the entry condition for the next: a student who has already interrogated a script arrives at modelling with a plan rather than a blank scene. The four stages do not carry equal weight in assessment. Final work is judged against the Creating stage, while the earlier stages are assessed formatively, which keeps the evaluative emphasis on original output without leaving the preparatory work unmonitored 35 . Text generation acts mainly by reducing extraneous load; image generation releases working-memory capacity that would otherwise be consumed by manual asset production; feedback guidance redirects the released capacity toward germane processing; and intrinsic load, fixed by the content itself, is left unchanged. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 Volunteers were recruited from second-year students in the animation programme of a comprehensive university. Eligibility required current enrolment in the core animation curriculum and no prior exposure to structured AIGCbased instruction, since the intervention presumes a comparable starting point in generative-tool familiarity 3 . Two intact classes served as the sampling frame, and allocation was made at class level, one class being assigned at random to the experimental condition and the other to the control. Randomising whole classes respected existing timetables, a pragmatic choice common in classroom-based research 28 ; with only two clusters, however, it cannot equate the groups in the way individual randomisation would, so the design is quasi-experimental and any class-level difference remains confounded with condition. The study is educational rather than clinical: participants were healthy students, the intervention was instructional, and all outcomes were educational measures. Approval from the institutional review board was obtained, and every participant gave written informed consent before baseline testing. The experimental group received the AIGC-driven LTAC integrated animation instruction, whereas the control group followed conventional animation teaching built around demonstration and guided practice 38 . Baseline equivalence was examined beforehand on sex ratio, age, prior animation experience, cognitive load, and creative thinking pretest scores. Categorical variables were compared with 𝜒𝜒 2 tests and continuous ones with independent-samples t tests; none of the comparisons was significant at p < 0.05, which is consistent with baseline equivalence without establishing it 30 . Table 2 reports these comparisons. As Table 2 indicates, the two groups did not differ appreciably on any measured attribute before instruction. That similarity makes a preexisting-difference account less plausible for the effects reported later, though with two clusters it cannot exclude unmeasured class-level differences 23 . The intervention ran for twelve weeks at four class hours per week, forty-eight class hours in total, and the same instructor taught both groups so that delivery style was held constant. Cognitive load was captured with a subjective rating instrument that separates intrinsic, extraneous, and germane subscales and records each item on a nine-point Likert continuum. The single-item mental-effort rating introduced by Paas provided the response format 42 , while the item content of the three subscales followed the differentiated instrument of Leppink and colleagues, which recovers the three load types as distinct components 43 . Splitting the construct this way matters for the present design, since the hypothesised pathways treat the three loads as functionally distinct rather than interchangeable 34 . Divergent thinking was assessed with an abbreviated Torrance-type battery covering fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration-the four facets the hypothesised model targets 17 . The choice of a Chinese form deserves comment, because Chinese-language adaptations of the Torrance battery already exist: Rudowicz and colleagues reported inter-scorer and parallel-form reliabilities for a Chinese version three decades ago, and the instrument has been used with Chinese-speaking samples ever since 44 . That version was developed for primary-school children, however, and neither its item content nor its norms suit animation undergraduates. The battery used here therefore followed the published Chinese adaptation in task format and scoring logic, with item stems revised for an adult sample and re-checked by translation and backtranslation. A pilot study then screened the resulting forms: internal consistency was estimated with Cronbach's α and convergent validity with composite reliability and average variance extracted, all computed by standard psychometric formulas that need no restatement here. Table 4 reports the pilot results, which cleared the customary thresholds of 0.70 for reliability and 0.50 for average variance extracted. As Table 4 shows, every subscale held together well enough to justify treating its items as a coherent measure. analysis.discussion: Why did the AIGC-driven model pull extraneous load down while pushing germane load up? The answer lies in how generative tools rearrange the flow of information reaching working memory. When an open-source text tool renders a script's structure visible, students no longer spend effort parsing formatting conventions or reconstructing narrative scaffolding by hand; that housekeeping is offloaded, and the presentation-driven demand that ordinarily clutters early learning thins out 37 . The same logic extends to redundancy. Conventional animation instruction often forces learners to process the same content through several channels at once-verbal explanation layered over manual sketching-whereas the generative pipeline lets each channel do distinct work, trimming the duplicated processing that inflates extraneous load 13 . Freed capacity does not simply vanish, though. Fig. 9 Heatmap of standardized path coefficients linking the three cognitive load dimensions to the four creative thinking facets, with color intensity encoding effect magnitude and direction. Fig. 8 Scatter plot of creative thinking composite scores against intrinsic cognitive load, overlaid with the fitted quadratic curve. The vertex falls at a moderate load value, approximately 5.9 on the ninepoint scale, which is the pattern an inverted-U association implies. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 The generative activities in the Thinking and Creating stages demand that students evaluate, curate, and reassemble machine output, which is exactly the kind of effortful schema-building that germane load names 23 . The selective response of the facets asks for a different explanation. Fluency and flexibility trade largely on retrieval speed and category switching, capacities that improve with practice in either condition, so it is unsurprising that they rose in both groups without a group difference 28 . Originality and elaboration depend instead on deeper transformation-combining remote associates, refining a concept until it holds together-and these operations draw on precisely the schema-building resources that germane load names 30 . On this reading the intervention did not make students think more; it changed the quality of thinking that the freed capacity could sustain, which is why the advantage concentrated in the two facets most sensitive to deep processing. The correlations in Fig. 7 sharpen that account. Fluency and flexibility hang together closely, as they should if both index the breadth of an initial search through memory, and their joint insensitivity to condition suggests that the generative toolchain did not simply accelerate idea retrieval. Originality and elaboration form a separate and more moderate pairing, and their weak association with fluency matters for interpretation: had originality risen only because students produced more responses, its correlation with fluency should have been considerably higher than the 0.41 observed. The same two-part structure has emerged from factor analyses of the Torrance battery, where fluency-driven and transformation-driven components separate rather than collapse into a single dimension 31 . Set against the long-run decline in originality and elaboration documented for large samples, the present result reads as a modest counterpoint, since the facets hardest to move historically are the ones this intervention moved 46 . Ulger's finding that creative training can lift divergent-thinking scores without touching problem-solving is a useful caution in the other direction: facet-level gains need not generalise to the wider construct 29 . The inverted-U finding for intrinsic load carries a caution that the earlier sections could only foreshadow. Too little intrinsic challenge leaves creative reasoning underpowered, while too much saturates working memory and crowds out the generative operations creativity needs 34 . The practical lesson is that intrinsic load should be tuned rather than minimised. A teacher designing an AIGC-supported animation task ought to calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range-demanding enough to engage, restrained enough to leave room for exploration-rather than assuming that easier is always better 12 . This tempers a common but simplistic reading of load theory, and it is among the more transferable takeaways here. Set against prior work, these results are largely consonant but not identical. Studies pairing design thinking with germane load in STEAM settings likewise found creativity gains routed through deep engagement, which aligns with the mediation reported above 30 . The divergence lies in specificity: earlier flipped-learning and projectbased interventions reported broad creative-thinking improvement without partitioning which facets responded, so their apparent whole-scale gains may have masked the facet-level selectivity observed here 28 . Measurement grain is the likeliest reason for the discrepancy, since aggregating creativity into a single score can hide exactly the discriminant pattern that makes a mechanism legible 20 . Three implications follow for theory. The first concerns the status of germane load. Cognitive load theory has increasingly treated germane load as a redistribution of resources rather than an independent source of demand 14 , and the mediation estimate reported here gives that reconceptualisation an empirical foothold in a creative domain: germane load acted on originality and elaboration not directly but through a deep-processing strategy, which is what a redistribution account predicts. The second concerns the shape of the intrinsic-load effect. A curvilinear relation is hard to reconcile with the standard prescription to minimise load, and it suggests that the prescription was always domain-bound, holding for schema acquisition but not for tasks whose value lies in exploration. The third concerns creativity theory. Because the four facets responded differently to one instructional manipulation, treating divergent thinking as a single latent ability discards information that a facet-level model retains-an argument the creativity literature has long made on psychometric grounds 31 and that an intervention study can now make on experimental ones. For practice, the findings translate into three design rules rather than a general endorsement of generative tools. Assign generative assistance to the parts of a task that consume attention without building competence-formatting, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 rendering, asset production-and keep it away from the parts where the struggle is the point. Make sure something recruits the freed capacity, because a lighter task is not automatically a more generative one; in the LTAC model the curation, evaluation, and reassembly demanded in the Thinking and Creating stages did that work. And calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range instead of smoothing it away. For animation programmes weighing curricular reform, an open-source toolchain can lower barriers to production while raising the ceiling on deep creative work, but only where the instructional design treats load as something to shape rather than merely shed 32 . That conditional is the substantive message for anyone hoping to scale generative tools across higher education in art and design 3 . reading.overview: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in higher education; however, little is known about what its use means for adult learners’ digital well-being (DWB) and quality of life (QoL). This mixed-methods study, which leaned towards a qualitative design (qualitative dominant), investigated these issues among adult learners at a university in Ghana.
reading.findings: The results showed universal access to smartphones (99%), while 71% had access to a laptop. Adult learners in this cross-sectional survey reported a generally positive appraisal of their DWB. Overall, the DWB mean score (M = 4.58, SD = 0.76) is above the scale midpoint, indicating a favourable orientation towards GenAI use, although some variation exists across the well-being domains. The mental subscale showed modestly positive cognitive and psychosocial gains (M = 4.09, SD = 1.12), with the strongest item endorsements for improved problem-solving (M=4.94, SD=1.49), increased productivity (M=4.42, SD=1.59), greater decisiveness (M = 4.42, SD = 1.48) and feeling more cheerful (M = 4.42, SD = 1.64). The emotional subscale also reflected positive outcomes (M = 4.51, SD = 1.29), driven by items such as increased interest in new things (M = 5.08, SD = 1.46) and clearer thinking (M = 4.60, SD = 1.61). Following reverse coding, the physical DWB subscale recorded the highest mean (M = 5.14, SD = 1.45), with all indicators (sleep, eating, aches, and reduced exercise) scoring above the neutral point (4.93 ≤ M ≤ 5.37). However, item-level frequencies indicate that this pattern was not uniform. While most respondents selected the disagreement options, a minority reported physical strain: 17.0% reported disturbed sleep, 10.9% reported changes in eating habits, 16.5% reported physical discomfort, and 16.5% reported reduced physical exercise. Thus, although the overall trend suggests limited physical strain, less than half of the sample still experienced some bodily effects associated with GenAI use. For QoL, the composite mean (M = 2.06, SD = 0.94) shows that adult learners reported some improvement in daily functioning, safety, control, activity engagement, and time efficiency (Table 3). analysis.discussion: The rise of GenAI technologies in educational settings extends beyond instructional implications but also has consequential psychological impacts on the user. As accurately captured by Christodoulou and Zembylas23, technology acceptance is not a clear-cut matter of positive or negative attitudes but involves complicated stories and changes in relationships that affect the views and experiences of users. The present study attempts to address the gap in current literature on the lack of a comprehensive focus and understanding of the consequences of GenAI use on the “human side” of diverse cohorts of adult learners, particularly within the African/Ghanaian Taken together, findings from both the quantitative and qualitative phases paint a similar picture of how adult learners in the study perceive their DWB and QoL when interacting with GenAI. In the two phases of the study, adult learners' engagement with GenAI is characterised by coexisting gains and strain and not just a uniformly positive or negative experience. In the quantitative phase, DWB mean score was slightly above the 7-point Likert scale midpoint, with a meaningful minority of respondents reporting physical strain, and the composite mean of QoL indicated only modest gains in some aspects of GenAI-supported learning. The qualitative phase of the study throws further light on the mixed results in the survey; collaborators reflected on both appreciation for GenAI’s efficiency and anxiety over its encroachment on human creativity and authenticity. Using the unified ecological framework as a lens to understand the reciprocal and dynamic interrelationships between individuals, digital platforms, physical spaces, and macro-level factors, both findings highlight that adult learners’ DWB is a function of these interrelated factors. First, results from the survey and storytelling reveal that adult learners are knowledgeable of digital tools (including GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, etc.) and, on average, possess digital skills and competencies which they use to interact meaningfully across several digital platforms (i.e. Google, learning management systems). Second, interaction on digital platforms occurs at multiple levels and at different physical places (e.g. home, school setting) for some purposeful outcomes. Positive outcomes through GenAI use reflect gains (manifested as strengths) whilst the negative experiences Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:37204 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78289-5 14 and outcomes create digital anxieties (afflictions). Third, GenAI use within the higher education context is constrained or limited by institutional-level factors (macro-level) such as policies on GenAI use, access to digital platforms and type of engagement. Thus, institutional factors mediate and shape adult learners' use of GenAI within this context. As such, adult learners' experiences of the extent to which their level of need and satisfaction is met through GenAI use reveal their state of well-being/wellness. Furthermore, both results highlight that within the higher education context, adult learners’ use of GenAI on a variety of digital platforms to perform academic and non-academic tasks is pervasive. Multiple digital connectivity at different places fosters a continuous cycle of constantly and actively creating and recreating their digital experiences, leading to cognitive and affective gains as well as embodied strains. Through such a process, they develop several coping systems which are mostly culturally embedded to counteract and adjust to the unpleasant physical afflictions. In sum, adult learners' digital well-being occurs through these nested multiple layers of influence (at the individual, meso and macro-levels), and is sustained by the powerful functionalities In addition, the results reveal that adult learners' positive gains with GenAI usage moderately influenced their cognitive, affective, and psychosocial well-being. For example, the qualitative arm of the study showed that adult learners appreciated the powerful functionalities of GenAI through enhanced efficiency in learning, but expressed psychological strain and apprehension. While it is true that GenAI tools like ChatGPT can enhance cognitive tasks, for instance, by making problem-solving activities easier, improving self-efficacy for task resolution and enhancing the quality and originality of solutions83, blind usage does not foster critical thinking and problem-solving, which are essential for academic and lifelong success15. Furthermore, the study found that some adult learners experienced minimal effects on their physical well-being as a result of GenAI usage, necessitating the development of self-adaptive coping mechanisms to alleviate the negative impacts of their digital experiences. Inferring from the unified ecological framework8, which illustrates a linkage between physical and digital domains influencing DWB when interacting with AI, the results imply that while GenAI usage may confer mental and emotional advantages, these are accompanied by modest but consistent reports of adverse bodily effects. Past studies have suggested that GenAI can reduce stress by streamlining tasks or creating a stress-free and emotionally supportive learning environment42,43,84, but excessive use of such technologies can lead to heightened anxiety, burnout, and sleep disturbance85. The survey results further showed that adult learners' experience of unstable internet connectivity and institutional policies inhibit their experiences with GenAI usage and moderately impact their physical well- being. Drawing on the unified ecological framework, this finding highlights the interconnections between physical spaces and macro-social factors which directly or indirectly influence adult learners' well-being. The physical place comprises different built and natural characteristics8. Studies show that the non-human elements in the physical setting impact people’s (students’) well-being in various ways86,87. Within the physical space, in this case, the school (or university environment), which is a digital learning environment, IT infrastructure and reliable internet access are critical to moderating and sustaining interactions at all levels- micro, meso and macro-levels. Institution-wide policies on IT and data usage in teaching and learning mediate peer-to- peer (micro) interactions as well as meso-level interactions (i.e. student–lecturer relationships). items.abstract_text: ABSTRACT Background As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reshapes the learning process, students will inevitably experience cognitive conflicts when their existing knowledge and beliefs clash with information provided by GenAI. Improper handling of cognitive conflicts may lead to a decline in students' learning efficiency and even hinder the development of critical thinking skills. Objective This study aims to understand how students respond to cognitive conflicts during their interactions with GenAI, with a focus on comparing high‐performing and low‐performing student groups. Methods To identify relationships between cognitive conflict intensity and students' responses, we used a covariate‐dependent Markov chain (a sequential data modelling method) to analyse the response states of 411 students in a simulated academic writing task and observed transitions in student response states across different task performances. Results The results revealed that the intensity of cognitive conflict had a significant impact on students' state transitions. Overall, as the level of conflict increased, students' state changes exhibited a phased pattern, shifting from fluctuation (transitioning to a variety of different states) to inertia or convergence (maintaining the original state or transitioning uniformly to a negative response state). Student response state transitions varied across different task performance levels. Conclusions This study provides a novel methodological perspective for modelling sequential response dynamics in Human‐AI interaction. The findings offer new insights into the cognitive conflict dynamics in GenAI‐assisted learning, providing implications for designing GenAI‐assisted learning environments.

items.title: Cognitive Predictors of AI-Related Textual Change in Upper-Intermediate L2 Russian Writing: Working Memory, Attention Control, and Critical Thinking

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can alter final second-language (L2) texts, yet cognitive differences may shape which changes emerge. This exploratory study examined 38 upper-intermediate learners of Russian who each produced one composition with AI assistance and one without it. Working memory, attention control, and critical thinking were measured continuously, and 11 textual outcomes were calculated from paired compositions. AI-assisted texts showed higher lemma-based lexical-diversity values, longer words, more connectives per 100 words, and substantially fewer first-person markers, while total word count, sentence measures, and formulaic-expression rate did not differ in the full sample. The higher POS-based content-word density was attenuated after first-person forms were excluded, suggesting a contribution from the change in person marking. Exploratory models suggested negative working-memory associations with lexical-diversity and connective-rate change, and negative attention-control associations with lexical-diversity change. The positive working-memory coefficient for word-count change was sensitive to HC3 estimation and leave-one-out refitting. Critical thinking showed no clear independent association in the primary change-score models, while positive coefficients for MATTR and HD-D appeared in the outcome-conditioned models. Under this supervised, student-mediated procedure, AI assistance was associated with lexical, discourse-marking, and stance differences in completed L2 texts.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: AI-mediated teaching requires teachers to evaluate uncertain information, respond to changing conditions, and integrate AI with pedagogical judgment. This study examined four cognitive-professional resource domains relevant to intelligent professional action: digital literacy, digital resilience, AI-mediated epistemic agency (AMEA), and AI-TPACK. Variable-centered and person-centered analyses drew on a cross-sectional survey of 942 YouShi Plan preservice teachers at one Chinese university. Perceived structured teacher-education support was positively associated with all four resources. Self-reported teaching innovation competence was positively associated with jointly higher digital literacy and digital resilience, with the response surface primarily reflecting their combined level. Four resource profiles mainly differed in overall level and showed graded differences in perceived teaching innovation competence. Higher perceived support was also associated with membership in higher-resource profiles. Together, these findings connect perceived teacher-education support, cognitive-professional resource configurations, and self-reported teaching innovation competence, positioning the latter as a domain-specific perceived capability relevant to intelligent professional action in AI-mediated teaching.

items.abstract_text: This study investigates the factors associated with university students’ intention to use Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in Ghana, with particular attention to the role of psychological barriers in shaping technology use intention. This study extends the UTAUT model by incorporating the concept of digital learning anxiety in understanding the psychological dimension of students using generative AI. The study employed a quantitative approach using a cross-sectional survey design, with data analyzed through covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). The sample consisted of 350 university students in Ghana. Structural equation modeling and a bias-corrected percentile bootstrapping method were conducted in AMOS (v 23) to estimate the path coefficients. The results showed that performance expectancy and effort expectancy were positively associated with students’ intention to use GenAI. Additionally, a significant but small indirect association was found between effort expectancy and behavioral intention through digital learning anxiety. However, the findings indicate the insignificant influence of social influence. This study contributes to the literature by providing context-specific evidence from Ghanaian higher education on the role of Digital Learning Anxiety in students’ intention to use GenAI. However, because the study used cross-sectional data, this indirect relationship should be interpreted as an association rather than evidence of a causal mechanism. The findings suggest that students’ intention to use GenAI is associated with both their perceptions of the technology and their psychological responses to its use. These findings provide context-specific evidence on GenAI acceptance among the students surveyed.

analysis.methods: The study employed a quantitative approach using a cross-sectional survey design, with data analyzed through covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). According to Creswell and Creswell (2018) , a cross-sectional survey examines the relationship between constructs within a population at a precise time. Data were collected at a single point in time to examine the relationships among the study variables. The study targeted undergraduate students from the College of Humanities at the public university in Ghana, encompassing departments such as English, Linguistics, and Communication Studies, with a total population of 3,200. These students were selected because their academic coursework is conducted substantially in English and involves language-intensive academic activities. A total of 350 undergraduate students participated in the study. The sample size of 350 was considered adequate for the specified CB-SEM model, given the model’s complexity and the number of observed indicators. SEM sample-size adequacy depends on factors such as model complexity, factor loadings, and estimation conditions rather than on a single universal sample-size rule ( Wolf et al., 2013 ). With this approach, respondents who were available and willing to respond to the questionnaire were finally selected for the study ( Sterner et al., 2024 ). The questionnaire was administered in paper format during scheduled lecture sessions to maximize participation. A cover letter accompanied the questionnaire, detailing the objectives of the study, the criteria for qualification (university students using digital tools), and an assurance of anonymity and confidentiality. The data collection began on November 10, 2025, and ended on December 2, 2025. After 3 weeks of the data collection process, 350 questionnaires were appropriately filled out and used for the analysis. From Table 1 , it was clear that Level 300 students dominated the study, constituting 41.1%, followed by Level 400 students with a percentage of 32.6%, and Level 200 students, who constituted 26.3%. Regarding gender, males constituted 54.3%, while females constituted 45.7%. A structured questionnaire was utilized to collect the data. Although the measurement items were adapted from prior studies, we piloted the questionnaire to determine the necessity of clarifying any ambiguous statements, particularly regarding technical AI terminology. The study was pilot-tested on a sample of 30 students, of whom 10 students were randomly selected from different lecture groups. With their comments and suggestions, the questionnaire was amended and subsequently used for the main data collection. The questionnaire had three sections. Part A consisted of the basic demographics: gender, age, and university level. Part B contained items measuring the UTAUT constructs of Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, and Social Influence. Items measuring these constructs were adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003) and contextualized to GenAI-supported learning. The third part, Part C, contained items measuring Digital Learning Anxiety (DLA) and Behavioral Intention (BI). The DLA items were adapted from the identified literature on technology- and AI-related anxiety and contextualized to Generative AI-supported learning, while the BI items were adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003) . All items were measured on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree). The measurement items and their corresponding sources are presented in Appendix A . Content validity was first established through expert review. The suitability of the draft instrument was assessed by three senior researchers and two lecturers in the Department of English and Linguistics. This assessment was done to check whether the items of measurement sounded ambiguous, were appropriate for the research objectives with regard to Generative AI, and whether the statements were clear to university students. From their suggestions, minor adjustments in wording were made in the items measuring Digital Learning Anxiety to make them even clearer. Following the assessment of content validity, statistical analysis through SPSS (v.23) was used to check the internal consistency of the constructs. Although Cronbach's alpha is widely reported, McDonald's Omega was adopted as the principal reliability coefficient because it provides a more robust estimate of internal consistency for latent variable models. As shown in Table 2 , the reliability analysis was conducted for the five core constructs: performance expectancy (PE), effort expectancy (EE), social influence (SI), digital learning anxiety (DLA), and behavioral intention (BI). It can be observed that all constructs demonstrated high internal consistency, with values above the commonly recommended threshold of 0.70 ( Hair et al., 2012 ). Effort Expectancy (EE) obtained the highest reliability ( ω = .969), followed by Digital Learning Anxiety ( ω = .966), Behavioral Intention ( ω = .957), and Performance Expectancy ( ω = .964). The lowest value, for Social Influence (SI), was still satisfactory at ω = .884. These results indicate satisfactory internal consistency among the items measuring the five constructs. To minimize common method bias, procedural and statistical actions were taken ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Participants were assured of their anonymity and that their answers would be treated on a confidential basis to avoid social desirability bias. In addition, the questionnaire items were separated into different sections to reduce response pattern tendencies. The single questionnaire was divided into several sections, each consisting of the corresponding items. The first unrotated factor accounted for 43.24% of the total variance. However, because Harman's single-factor test provides only a limited diagnostic of common method bias, this result was not treated as conclusive evidence that common method bias was absent ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Although procedural remedies and Harman's single-factor assessment were used to assess the possibility of common method bias, Harman's test alone cannot conclusively establish the absence of such bias. Therefore, the results should not be interpreted as demonstrating that common method bias has been completely eliminated. Exploratory Factor Analysis was conducted using the SPSS statistical package version 23. EFA was conducted to examine the underlying factor structure of the measurement items and to assess whether the observed variables loaded onto their intended latent constructs. EFA helps to uncover the possible link between the variables; it identifies the underlying dimension
analysis.discussion: This study examined the associations of traditional UTAUT constructs and Digital Learning Anxiety with university students’ intention to use Generative AI. The findings showed that Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. These findings provide context-specific evidence that both cognitive evaluations and affective responses are relevant to understanding students’ intention to use GenAI. Among the predictors examined, Performance Expectancy had the largest positive standardized association with Behavioral Intention. This finding indicates that students primarily evaluate Generative AI based on its perceived ability to improve their academic performance. This finding is consistent with the original UTAUT model, which identifies performance expectancy as the strongest determinant of technology adoption ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). The present study extends this evidence to Generative AI within a Ghanaian higher-education context, suggesting that students primarily consider the perceived educational value of GenAI when forming their intention to use it. This reinforces the argument that students evaluate AI according to its educational value and contribution to learning outcomes. Regarding language learning, Matthews (2024) argued that interaction becomes more fluid for students who view AI as a cognitive partner that assists with outlines or syntax. Furthermore, the significant positive association of Effort Expectancy suggests that the nature of the interaction is defined by its accessibility. The natural language processing (NLP) abilities of large language models allow for a plug-and-play experience that is far simpler than traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS), which often require technical training ( Karahan and Bilgili, 2025 ). Furthermore, the significant positive association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention suggests that perceived ease of interaction is relevant to students’ intention to use GenAI. The natural-language interface of many GenAI systems may make interaction more accessible than technologies requiring greater technical familiarity. However, the present study did not directly compare GenAI with other educational technologies. Contrary to the original UTAUT model, Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. This finding suggests that Social Influence did not explain additional variation in students’ intention to use GenAI after the other predictors in the model were considered. The finding differs from the traditional UTAUT proposition that social influence contributes to technology acceptance ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). However, the present study did not examine the specific social circumstances surrounding students’ GenAI use. Therefore, the reason for the non-significant relationship cannot be established from the present data. Future research could examine how lecturer expectations, peer influence, institutional norms, and students’ patterns of GenAI use may help explain the role of Social Influence in GenAI acceptance. A key finding of this study was the significant negative association between Digital Learning Anxiety and students’ intention to use Generative AI (H5). Effort Expectancy was also negatively associated with Digital Learning Anxiety (H4), indicating that students who perceived GenAI as easier to use tended to report lower levels of anxiety. These findings are consistent with Karal and Özdemir (2025) and Kristandl (2025) , who identified AI-related anxiety as relevant to students’ engagement with Generative AI. However, the cross-sectional nature of the present data does not establish the direction or causal nature of these relationships. The mediation analysis showed that lower Effort Expectancy was associated with higher Digital Learning Anxiety, while higher Digital Learning Anxiety was associated with lower Behavioral Intention. The indirect association was statistically significant but small; however, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causality among these variables. The findings contribute to research on GenAI acceptance by showing that affective responses may be considered alongside traditional UTAUT constructs. Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence, however, did not explain additional variation in Behavioral Intention within the specified structural model. These findings suggest that models of GenAI acceptance may benefit from considering students’ affective responses alongside their evaluations of usefulness and ease of use. The significant indirect association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention through Digital Learning Anxiety also provides evidence for examining affective processes alongside UTAUT predictors. However, this indirect association was small, accounting for approximately 11% of the total association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention. Most of the association was therefore direct. Moreover, because the variables were measured at the same point in time, the indirect association should not be interpreted as evidence that Effort Expectancy causes changes in Digital Learning Anxiety or that anxiety subsequently causes changes in Behavioral Intention. The findings suggest some practical considerations that may be examined further in the design of GenAI-supported learning environments. Given the positive association between Performance Expectancy and Behavioral Intention, universities may consider helping students understand the potential academic uses and limitations of GenAI. Similarly, the associations involving Effort Expectancy and Digital Learning Anxiety suggest that accessible guidance and opportunities to become familiar with GenAI may be worth investigating as possible ways of supporting students’ engagement with these technologies. Universities may also consider providing low-stakes opportunities in which students can explore appropriate uses of GenAI and receive guidance on academic integrity and responsible use. However, the present cross-sectional findings do not demonstrate that such interventions will increase GenAI adoption or reduce anxiety. These suggestions should therefore be treated as design hypotheses that require evaluation through experimental, longitudinal, or intervention-based research. This study
analysis.limitations: Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. First, the cross-sectional design does not permit the establishment of long-term causal relationships. Because Effort Expectancy, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention were measured at the same point in time, the indirect relationship identified in the model does not establish temporal or causal mediation. Reverse relationships and unmeasured factors that may influence these constructs cannot be ruled out. Accordingly, the observed indirect association may also reflect alternative directional relationships or common causes that were not included in the model. Additionally, because all measures were collected using self-reported responses, the findings may be influenced by respondents’ subjective perceptions. Although statistical procedures were employed to assess the validity and reliability of the measurement model, future studies may benefit from combining survey data with behavioral or observational measures of AI usage. The use of convenience sampling also limits the representativeness of the sample. Because participants were recruited during scheduled lecture sessions, students who were absent during data collection were less likely to be represented. The findings should therefore not be generalized to all university students in Ghana without caution. The structural model did not include potential control variables such as gender, university level, prior GenAI experience, device access, or English proficiency. Some of these factors may be associated with students’ perceptions of GenAI, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention. Consequently, the observed relationships may partly reflect unmeasured confounding, and future studies should examine the robustness of these associations after accounting for relevant demographic, technological, and language-related characteristics. Although the study was conducted among university students in an English-medium academic setting and the questionnaire included items contextualized to language-related academic activities, English proficiency and L2-specific psychological constructs were not directly measured. The findings should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that the observed relationships are specifically attributable to students’ English proficiency or L2-related anxiety. Again, the rapidly evolving nature of generative AI limits the temporal stability of the findings. By targeting humanities students in one academic setting, it becomes difficult to establish the effectiveness in other disciplines, such as STEM. Moreover, the convenience sampling approach may have introduced selection bias because participation depended on students’ availability and willingness to respond. Finally, the quantitative design did not permit an in-depth exploration of students’ lived experiences when interacting with Generative AI. Future qualitative studies could provide richer insights into these experiences. Future studies could extend the framework by examining additional factors such as Academic Integrity Awareness and investigating whether the observed relationships differ across academic disciplines. Longitudinal research could examine how students’ AI-related anxiety and acceptance change as their experience with GenAI develops over time. Qualitative research may also provide deeper insight into the social and institutional factors associated with students’ decisions to use GenAI. Finally, empirical studies examining the effects of GenAI-supported learning on students’ actual academic performance and AI-use behaviour would provide a more balanced understanding of its educational implications. analysis.discussion: Based on five-wave longitudinal data, this study used parallel-process latent growth models to examine the developmental relationships among classroom engagement, flow experience, and musical emotional intelligence. All three variables showed significant positive growth, with significant individual differences in growth rates. Growth in classroom engagement was significantly positively related to growth in flow experience, and growth in flow experience was likewise significantly positively related to growth in musical emotional intelligence. Further growth mediation analyses showed that growth in flow experience had a significant longitudinal indirect effect between growth in classroom engagement and growth in musical emotional intelligence. These core relationships remained stable after controlling for students’ background characteristics and initial levels. Classroom engagement, flow experience, and musical emotional intelligence all showed significant positive developmental trends across the five measurement occasions. In the unconditional growth models, the mean slopes of the three variables were all significantly greater than zero, and the slope variances were all significant. Thus, within the learning period covered by this study, the three variables not only changed overall but also differed noticeably in their pace of development across students. Compared with level differences at a single time point, these growth trajectories more directly capture how students change over sustained learning. The growth in classroom engagement indicates that students’ investment in classroom tasks is not a fixed state but adjusts with ongoing learning experiences. As students become more familiar with task formats and classroom expectations, their ways of participating may also stabilize. Flow experience showed a similar developmental pattern. Sustained learning gives students opportunities to continually adjust the match between their abilities and task demands and to form more stable attention investment and activity absorption. The growth in musical emotional intelligence reflects that emotional abilities themselves have room for development. Music learning continuously involves perceiving emotional information in music and regulating one’s own emotional states, and these experiences accumulate through repeated practice. Musical emotional intelligence is therefore not merely a stable characteristic students have already formed before entering the classroom. The significant slope variance of all three variables also deserves attention. An overall average increase does not mean that all students follow the same developmental pattern. Some students improved relatively quickly during the study, while others changed more modestly. The parallel-process growth model builds on such individual differences in development to further examine whether different processes of change are interrelated. This study therefore asks whether a student’s speed of change in one psychological process is related to their speed of change in another psychological process. The positive relationship between growth in classroom engagement and growth in flow experience supported H1. In the three-process model, the classroom engagement slope was significantly positively correlated with the flow slope. In the growth mediation model, the path between engagement growth and flow growth also remained significant. Compared with the relationship whereby students with higher engagement at a given time point also have higher flow, this study reveals a connection between two psychological processes in terms of their rates of change. Students whose classroom engagement grew faster also tended to show faster growth in flow experience. Classroom engagement and flow represent different aspects of learning, and their linked growth suggests that sustained participation may provide more opportunities for concentration and task absorption. A higher level of engagement does not necessarily produce flow, but sustained increases in engagement can increase students’ opportunities to engage with tasks, process feedback, and adjust their performance. When students can invest more stably in the current task, the conditions needed to maintain attention and form activity absorption also increase. The relationship between classroom engagement and flow is therefore evident not only in level differences but also in its clear developmental properties. The significant relationship between growth in flow experience and growth in musical emotional intelligence supported H2. In the three-process model, the two slopes were significantly positively correlated, and in the growth mediation model, the path between flow growth and musical emotional intelligence growth was likewise significant. One important feature that distinguishes music learning from general knowledge learning is that the learning process itself continuously involves emotional information. When performing, listening, or composing, students not only need to complete tasks but also need to perceive musical expression and continually adjust their own emotional states. The sustained attention and deep absorption of flow allow learners to maintain processing of such information for extended periods. As deep immersive experience strengthens over the course of learning, processing experiences related to musical emotions may also accumulate in parallel. The key point here is not that flow itself equals musical emotional intelligence, but that the developmental processes of the two are systematically connected. Repeated experiences of flow during music learning may provide opportunities for students to recognize and regulate their emotions during practice and performance. This study therefore advances the relationship between flow and musical emotional intelligence from psychological covariation at a single time point to a connection between rates of development. The results for H3 further connected the first two sets of relationships. The path between growth in classroom engagement and growth in flow was significant, the path between growth in flow and growth in musical emotional intelligence was significant, and the bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval of the indirect effect did not include zero. After including growth in flow, the direct path between growth in classroom engagement and growth in musical emotional intelligence was no longer significant. The developmental link between classroom engagement and musical emotional intelligence is therefore partly embodied in the concurrent development of flow experience. items.abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can provide preservice teachers with a complete lesson plan before they have articulated the reasoning the plan is intended to develop, creating conditions for automation bias and cognitive offloading. This multiple-case study examined how five preservice mathematics teachers in China negotiated epistemic authority while planning using GenAI. Methods Cases were selected from 42 preservice teachers through preliminary quantitative screening. Screen-recording-derived event logs, concurrent verbalizations, video-stimulated recall interviews, and written reflections were integrated into an evidence matrix comprising 34 decision episodes. Authority was interpreted as retained, shared, or ceded based on the relationship among the source of a proposal, the participant’s action, the warrant invoked, and whether that warrant was enacted in the lesson plan. Results Authority was retained in 16 episodes, shared in 12, and ceded in 6, with variation across cases. Visible actions did not map onto authority positions in a fixed way, and professional warrants were sometimes not enacted. Two vulnerabilities emerged. A closed verification loop, observed in four episodes across two cases, occurred when participants recognized uncertainty about AI output yet asked the same AI to validate it. An insight–action gap, illustrated by three episodes in a single case, occurred when recognized pedagogica problems were not translated into planned teacher responses. Discussion The findings support the proposition that the educative value of AI-assisted planning depends less on how much novices edit AI output than on whether tasks require independent verification and warranted, enacted decisions.

reading.overview: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can provide preservice teachers with a complete lesson plan before they have articulated the reasoning the plan is intended to develop, creating conditions for automation bias and cognitive offloading. This multiple-case study examined how five preservice mathematics teachers in China negotiated epistemic authority while planning using GenAI.
reading.methods: The study used a qualitatively driven multiple-case design ( Yin, 2018 ) that was preceded by a quantitative screening phase. The screening phase served a single function: purposeful selection of cases through quantitatively informed maximum-variation sampling from a cohort of 42 preservice teachers ( Patton, 2015 ). In mixed-methods terms, the two phases were connected only at the sampling stage ( Creswell and Plano Clark, 2018 ). Screening data were not analyzed as a separate strand, did not generate hypotheses for the case analysis, and were not merged with the qualitative findings; they were used only to locate each focal case within the cohort distribution ( Table 1 ). The primary purpose of the case study was explanatory: to examine how epistemic authority shifted during AI-assisted lesson planning and what enabled those shifts. Each participant constituted a case. Cases were embedded, with individual planning episodes serving as subunits of analysis within each case. Focal cases and preliminary screening context. The study took place in a required undergraduate course, Study of Elementary Mathematics , within the third year of a four-year preservice mathematics teacher education program at a pseudonymized Chinese university (“Y University”). Y University was selected as the study site because members of the research team were faculty members there, which provided access to the program and familiarity with its curriculum. The focal task was completed after regular class
reading.findings: Authority varied within every case. Each of the five participants retained, shared, or ceded authority in different decisions, and no participant could be described by a single position ( Table 2 ). Across the 34 decision episodes, authority was retained in 16, shared in 12, and ceded in 6. As decisions differed in scope and importance, the counts indicate where evidence is located rather than how agentic each participant was, and they are not used to rank participants ( Table 2 ). Descriptive distribution of authority positions. The analysis identified three recurring patterns. First, complete AI-generated plans shifted plans by changing the starting task from constructing a lesson to deciding whether to accept one. Second, the most frequent visible actions did not correspond to a single authority position, and an articulated professional warrant was not always enacted in the plan. analysis.methods: The study used a qualitatively driven multiple-case design ( Yin, 2018 ) that was preceded by a quantitative screening phase. The screening phase served a single function: purposeful selection of cases through quantitatively informed maximum-variation sampling from a cohort of 42 preservice teachers ( Patton, 2015 ). In mixed-methods terms, the two phases were connected only at the sampling stage ( Creswell and Plano Clark, 2018 ). Screening data were not analyzed as a separate strand, did not generate hypotheses for the case analysis, and were not merged with the qualitative findings; they were used only to locate each focal case within the cohort distribution ( Table 1 ). The primary purpose of the case study was explanatory: to examine how epistemic authority shifted during AI-assisted lesson planning and what enabled those shifts. Each participant constituted a case. Cases were embedded, with individual planning episodes serving as subunits of analysis within each case. Focal cases and preliminary screening context. The study took place in a required undergraduate course, Study of Elementary Mathematics , within the third year of a four-year preservice mathematics teacher education program at a pseudonymized Chinese university (“Y University”). Y University was selected as the study site because members of the research team were faculty members there, which provided access to the program and familiarity with its curriculum. The focal task was completed after regular class hours on 17 March 2026 and did not count toward course assessment. Following identification during the preliminary quantitative screening, selected participants were invited to complete the task voluntarily. The task was completed within a suggested 45-min window. Participants could finish early or continue until they judged the plan complete. Researchers observed the task in person and additionally reviewed screen recordings retrospectively. Participants worked individually with an AI interface beside a Microsoft Word document and were asked to create a complete mathematics lesson plan. No template was imposed, and completeness was self-determined by each participant. They were instructed to select a junior-secondary topic. Suggested topics were slope, side-angle-side (SAS) triangle congruence proof, operations with negative numbers, and solving one-variable linear equations, although they could propose another topic. Participants could use any publicly accessible AI chat interface of their choosing. They also chose their own initial and subsequent prompts. Three participants used Doubao (ByteDance) and two used DeepSeek, all through the free public web interfaces on 17 March 2026. The deep-thinking function was enabled in T3’s session and the web-search function in T2’s session; neither function was enabled in the other sessions. No model version was recorded. As these interfaces are updated over time, the AI outputs analyzed here reflect the versions available on that date. All prompts submitted during the task are listed in Supplementary Table S1 . AI responses were not archived as text; they are visible in the screen recordings and are summarized for each episode in the evidence matrix ( Supplementary Table S2 ). Concurrent verbalization was encouraged to capture reactions and small decisions, but continuous think-aloud talk was not mandatory. The screening dataset contained complete records of questionnaire and performance tasks for 42 preservice mathematics teachers. The questionnaire was developed by the research team for this study. The four dimensions correspond to constructs discussed in research on AI literacy, epistemic vigilance, reliance on automation, cognitive offloading, achievement goal orientation, and epistemic agency ( Ames, 1992 ; Damsa et al., 2010 ; Long and Magerko, 2020 ; Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ; Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ; Scardamalia, 2002 ; Sperber et al., 2010 ). The composite used for case selection drew on 20 five-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) representing four dimensions each, with five items: critical evaluation of AI output (A1), AI dependence (A2), performative orientation (A3), and active reconstruction (A4). Before administration, the items were reviewed by a second researcher, who had not been involved in drafting them, for clarity and correspondence to their intended dimensions. Representative items include “I can judge whether the definitions or reasoning steps given by AI contain logical gaps” (A1), “I usually adopt AI-generated lesson-plan structures directly, without making any adjustments” (A2), “When designing a lesson plan, I give priority to whether it looks professional rather than whether I fully understand the content” (A3), and “I treat AI output as raw material and creatively reconstruct it rather than using it directly” (A4). Because the composite combined conceptually distinct dimensions, reliability was examined separately for each dimension. Reliability was acceptable to good for all four dimensions (Cronbach’s α = 0.73 for A1, 0.84 for A2, 0.72 for A3, and 0.71 for A4), with corrected item-total correlations ranging from 0.42 to 0.58 for A1, 0.56 to 0.75 for A2, 0.41 to 0.54 for A3, and 0.34 to 0.57 for A4. A1 and A4 were strongly positively correlated ( r = 0.70), and A2 and A3 were moderately positively correlated ( r = 0.40), but the two pairs were essentially unrelated to each other (| r | ≤ 0.08). Because A2 and A3 are negative dimensions—higher scores indicate more passive or dependent engagement—both were reverse-scored (6 − x , where 6 equals the sum of the scale’s minimum and maximum) before averaging, following standard procedures for handling reverse-worded items in composite scale scoring ( DeVellis, 2017 ; Spector, 1992 ). The composite agency score was computed as: Composite Agency Score = . Composite scores ranged from 2.70 to 4.45 ( M = 3.58). The performance task was developed by the research team for this study. The two content knowledge (CK) items were constructed from the treatment of slope and of the concept of function in the current junior-secondary mathematics textbooks, so that each proposition and correspondence relation concerned content that participants would be expected to teach. The AI-generated instructional content used in the three AI-evaluation items was produced using Claude (Anthropic) in response to prompts requesting worked explanations of junior-secondary topics. The research team then selected outputs that contained identifiable mathematical or conceptual-construction problems. analysis.results: Authority varied within every case. Each of the five participants retained, shared, or ceded authority in different decisions, and no participant could be described by a single position ( Table 2 ). Across the 34 decision episodes, authority was retained in 16, shared in 12, and ceded in 6. As decisions differed in scope and importance, the counts indicate where evidence is located rather than how agentic each participant was, and they are not used to rank participants ( Table 2 ). Descriptive distribution of authority positions. The analysis identified three recurring patterns. First, complete AI-generated plans shifted plans by changing the starting task from constructing a lesson to deciding whether to accept one. Second, the most frequent visible actions did not correspond to a single authority position, and an articulated professional warrant was not always enacted in the plan. Third, when participants were uncertain, authority tended to shift toward the AI, unless they could draw on professional resources, such as knowledge of student thinking or practicum experience. T1 began by asking Doubao for a Grade 8 lesson on the properties of parallelograms. The screen recording shows that she scrolled through the entire response once, then selected it all and pasted it into Word. In her written reflection, she explained: “I thought there was no major problem with the overall framework, but I was not very sure that it was a good design, so I accepted it”. The AI plan became the default trajectory before she had articulated a mathematical or pedagogical criterion. This episode was coded as ceding authority. T1’s later decisions, however, showed a different pattern. After reviewing the plan she pasted, she noticed that it did not address how students might respond during the activities or how the teacher should respond in turn. She entered a follow-up prompt: “You overlooked anticipated student responses and response strategies in your design”. Drawing on the content that Doubao then generated, she added anticipated student responses and response strategies to the activities in her Word document. This decision was coded as shared: T1 identified the gap and selected what to include, but the AI supplied most of the substantive content. However, for the proof of the second property, T1 did not rely on the AI’s content. The AI’s plan presented complete teacher demonstrations of both proofs. T1 reorganized this sequence so that the teacher would model the first proof, after which students would attempt the second proof themselves by drawing on the first. She typed a new teacher–student activity directly into the Word document: “The teacher asks students to discuss in groups how to prove the property, and invites a student to write the proof on the board”. For this activity, she did not adopt the anticipated responses that Doubao had generated. Instead, she wrote her own: “Students have gained experience from the previous proof and know that the property can be proved by showing that triangles are congruent.” In the stimulated-recall interview, she explained that after the teacher’s model, students should be able to “draw inferences from one case to another.” This interview account was consistent with the anticipated response she had outlined during planning. The reconstruction was coded as retained. The shift, therefore, was not from using AI to not using it. Rather, it was a shift from accepting an entire plan because it appeared coherent to redesigning part of it based on how students might reason. T3 began from the opposite position. Before prompting DeepSeek, he divided the lesson into four modules: objectives, key and difficult points, materials, and lesson content. His reflection explained: “If I have my own framework first, I can keep adjusting it”. He then asked the AI to fill these modules one at a time. For example, he first requested objectives for a lesson on SAS triangle congruence, then asked the AI to shorten and summarize them, and only after settling the objectives and key points did he ask for a sequence of lesson activities based on them. This teacher-authored structure determined what the AI was asked to generate and in what order, and it was coded as retained. Within this structure, most of T3’s subsequent decisions involved working with AI-generated content rather than replacing it. He asked the AI to anticipate students’ possible answers and simulate the classroom interaction for the introduction. For the “standard proof writing” segment, he asked the AI what students should pay particular attention to when writing proofs. Then he used its answer to add notes on format, the correspondence of conditions, and the completeness of conditions. In some places, however, he contributed content of his own. For the AI-generated variation exercises, he used a mathematical drawing tool to create figures that matched each problem’s conditions. The framework did not guarantee continued control. When he reached the “hands-on exploration” segment late in the session, the screen recording shows he hesitated for a long time before engaging with the AI-generated activity. In his recall interview, he explained that time was running short and that he did not know how to design the activity himself. No independent mathematical or pedagogical warrant for the activity appeared in any source, and the decision was therefore coded as ceded under the first criterion. His reflection suggested an awareness of this risk: accepting the AI’s wording, he wrote, could lead him to “gradually enter its rhythm”. T3’s case thus shows that a teacher-authored framework can support authority over the overall structure of a lesson without preventing local shifts back toward the AI. These cases address RQ1 in two ways. First, T1’s case shows that a complete AI-generated plan can change a novice’s starting task from constructing a lesson to deciding whether to accept one. Second, neither case settled into a stable position of authority. T1 later reclaimed authority by redesigning part of the plan, whereas T3, who began with his own framework, later adopted AI-generated content without a visible warrant. Authority thus shifted in both directions over the course of a single planning session. Across all five cases, this movement exhibited a temporal pattern: two of the six ceded episodes were the first episode of a case (T1, T5), in which a complete AI plan was adopted, and the remaining four occurred later in the planning session.
