analysis.discussion: The first contribution of this study concerns how GenAI changes the starting conditions of learning to plan. A complete AI plan did not simply supply ideas. It shifted planning from constructing an instructional trajectory to authorizing a ready-made one. T1’s first action was not an absence of participation—she prompted, copied, and formatted—but the mathematical or pedagogical criterion for accepting the plan remained unarticulated. Later reconstruction restored part of the reasoning work that planning is meant to develop. T3’s case followed the opposite order. His self-authored framework initially kept this reasoning work with him, but it did not prevent him from later adopting an AI-generated activity without a visible warrant. From a psychological perspective, T1’s initial acceptance is consistent with research on automation bias, in which people rely on automated recommendations instead of evaluating the available information themselves ( Goddard et al., 2012 ; Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ). Her reflection that she was “not very sure that it was a good design” but still accepted it suggests that the apparent coherence of the AI output supplanted her own evaluation. As automation bias was not measured as a psychological construct in this study, this is an interpretation informed by that research rather than evidence of the effect itself. However, this reliance was not fixed. Once she noticed a specific gap in the plan, she moved from accepting the output to revising it. This finding adds to existing research on preservice teachers and GenAI. Previous studies have mainly examined preservice teachers’ AI-related knowledge (AI-TPACK), their perceptions of the benefits of GenAI, and their integration of it into lesson planning ( Aldemir et al., 2025 ; Hsu et al., 2024 ; Kılıçkaya and Kic-Drgas, 2025 ). These aspects remain important, but they do not show which instructional decisions preservice teachers actually make for themselves when AI is involved. Nor does visible human participation guarantee the kind of hybrid intelligence envisioned in human-AI collaboration ( Cukurova, 2025 ). The present cases show that participation in the process alone is not enough to meet this condition. These cases point to a more demanding standard: preservice teachers should be able to identify, warrant, and assume responsibility for consequential instructional decisions. The finding also contributes to practice-based teacher education. Approximations are valuable when they preserve the core work novices need to learn ( Grossman et al., 2009 ). Simulation-based environments similarly create protected opportunities to rehearse decisions and examine their consequences ( Dieker et al., 2014 ; Ke and Xu, 2020 ). We propose that AI-assisted planning is more likely to remain an approximation of practice when the task requires preservice teachers to decompose the problem, anticipate students, compare alternatives, and justify transformations. A task that simply asks for a complete lesson plan may allow the AI to do much of this work. A task that asks preservice teachers to examine an AI plan and revise it against explicit professional criteria is more likely to help them retain this work. The second contribution is a decision-level account of professional judgment in lesson planning. The findings show that judgment could not be inferred from the amount of prompting or editing because the same visible action carried different meanings across episodes. Prompting the AI could keep authority with the participant or leave the AI as the substantive source. Retaining an AI proposal could follow deliberate comparison or unexamined trust. Recognizing a missing response could demonstrate pedagogical awareness while leaving AI’s plan unchanged. As warrant and enactment are part of how authority was defined, the substantive finding is that neither the type nor the amount of visible activity tracked these criteria. This finding brings research on epistemic agency into direct contact with professional judgment and professional noticing. Epistemic agency has emphasized responsibility for knowledge advancement and the negotiation of what counts as legitimate knowledge ( Damsa et al., 2010 ; Scardamalia, 2002 ; Stroupe, 2014 ). In lesson planning, the knowledge object is prospective practice. Responsibility is therefore visible when a teacher’s mathematical, curricular, pedagogical, or feasibility judgment changes what students would encounter. This interpretation is consistent with accounts of teacher judgment and noticing in which teachers attend to consequential information, interpret it through professional knowledge, and connect it to action ( Shulman, 1987 ; van Es and Sherin, 2008 ; Jacobs et al., 2010 ). The source-action-warrant-enactment sequence offers a way to observe that responsibility without treating AI contribution as inherently displacing or teacher editing as inherently agentic. The decision-level analysis also qualifies participant typologies. Song et al. (2025) identified useful patterns and levels in teachers’ GenAI integration, but the present cases show that professional authority can vary across different objects within the same planning session. T1 both ceded and retained authority; T4 both enacted a student-oriented sequencing decision and left other pedagogical insights outside the plan. Typologies may summarize broad orientations, but they should not be assumed to describe every professional decision. In these cases, ecological agency offered a more plausible account of this variation than a stable user trait ( Priestley et al., 2015 ). In the present cases, knowledge of student thinking, practicum experience, mathematical structure, and judgment about lesson capacity enabled authority to remain with the preservice teacher. Uncertainty about content or curriculum, limited teaching experience, and the fluent completeness of AI output made independent evaluation more difficult. Authority therefore had to be re-established for each consequential decision rather than secured once for the whole task. The third contribution is methodological: claims about professional judgment require evidence of how decisions developed. In this study, the screen recordings established what participants did and in what order, while the interviews and reflections supplied, extended, or complicated their reasons. Together, these sources revealed two vulnerabilities that would have been difficult to identify from final plans alone. The two differ in empirical breadth. items.abstract_text: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.

reading.interpretation: The present study examined the associations among generative AI dependency, effort regulation, and perceived learning outcomes among university students. GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes and was negatively associated with effort regulation, whereas effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes. The overall negative association included a statistically significant negative indirect component involving effort regulation, while the residual direct association was small, positive in sign, and not statistically significant. The primary latent-variable model indicated a small negative total association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. Although this association was statistically significant under the assumption of independent observations, its magnitude was limited ( β = −0.087), and the upper bound of its confidence interval was close to zero. The result therefore suggests only a modest relationship at the individual level and should not be interpreted as evidence of a substantial educational disadvantage associated with GenAI dependency. Moreover, because potential clustering within instructional classes was not accounted for, the precision of the estimated association may have been overstated. After effort regulation was included in the structural model, the residual direct association was not statistically significant. This pattern should not be interpreted as demonstrating that effort regulation fully explains the overall association or that the observed indirect association represents a causal mechanism. The complete questionnaire, including the Chinese wording used in data collection and corresponding English translations, is provided in Supplementary Appendix S1 . Generative AI dependency was assessed using a Chinese-language adaptation of the 11-item Generative AI Dependency Scale (GAIDS; Goh et al., 2025 ) prepared for the present study. The GAIDS comprises three dimensions: cognitive preoccupation (3 items), negative consequences (4 items), and withdrawal (4 items). The original scale demonstrated a stable three-factor structure and supported a higher-order generative AI dependency construct. Consistent with this conceptualization, the three first-order dimensions were modeled as indicators of a higher-order GenAI dependency construct in the structural analysis. A sample item is, “My decisions are often influenced by generative AI.” All items were scored in the same direction, with higher scores indicating greater generative AI dependency. Effort regulation was assessed using a Chinese-language adaptation of the four-item Effort Regulation subscale of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ; Pintrich et al., 1991 ), prepared for the present study. The subscale assesses students’ persistence and regulation of effort when learning tasks are difficult or uninteresting. The MSLQ was developed for assessing college students’ motivational orientations and learning strategies, including resource-management strategies. A sample item is, “Even when I do not like what I am learning, I still work hard to learn it well.” The original MSLQ uses a seven-point response scale. For the present study, a five-point format was adopted to maintain a consistent response structure across the questionnaire. Because changing the response format may affect measurement properties, the adapted measure was evaluated through internal consistency reliability, confirmatory factor analysis, and convergent and discriminant validity assessments. Although the results supported its use in the present sample, measurement equivalence with the original seven-point scale was not established. analysis.discussion: The present study examined the associations among generative AI dependency, effort regulation, and perceived learning outcomes among university students. GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes and was negatively associated with effort regulation, whereas effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes. The overall negative association included a statistically significant negative indirect component involving effort regulation, while the residual direct association was small, positive in sign, and not statistically significant. The primary latent-variable model indicated a small negative total association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. Although this association was statistically significant under the assumption of independent observations, its magnitude was limited ( β = −0.087), and the upper bound of its confidence interval was close to zero. The result therefore suggests only a modest relationship at the individual level and should not be interpreted as evidence of a substantial educational disadvantage associated with GenAI dependency. Moreover, because potential clustering within instructional classes was not accounted for, the precision of the estimated association may have been overstated. After effort regulation was included in the structural model, the residual direct association was not statistically significant. This pattern should not be interpreted as demonstrating that effort regulation fully explains the overall association or that the observed indirect association represents a causal mechanism. Previous research has associated GenAI dependency with procrastination, cognitive failures, poorer task performance, and weaker critical thinking ( Goh et al., 2025 ), while greater AI dependence has also been associated with lower critical thinking among university students ( Tian and Zhang, 2025 ). AI over-reliance has likewise been linked to less favorable learning performance ( Gao et al., 2026 ). However, these outcomes are not equivalent to perceived learning. The present study assessed students’ perceived cognitive, behavioral, and affective learning gains rather than objectively demonstrated achievement. Because perceived learning and independently assessed performance may diverge ( Deslauriers et al., 2019 ), the findings cannot establish whether GenAI dependency is similarly associated with objective learning outcomes. The present data cannot fully disentangle these subjective and objective dimensions, and the nonsignificant residual direct association should not be interpreted as evidence that GenAI dependency is educationally inconsequential. GenAI dependency was negatively associated with effort regulation, consistent with emerging evidence connecting AI dependency with self-regulatory functioning. Liu and Liu (2026) reported a negative association between metacognitive self-regulation and GenAI dependency, and Liu (2026) similarly identified a negative association between broader self-regulated learning and AI dependence among frequent AIGC users. More directly, Maizel et al. (2026) identified stronger effort regulation as being associated with lower AI dependency. In the present study, effort regulation was in turn positively associated with perceived learning outcomes, consistent with the role of persistence and resource management in academic functioning ( Pintrich, 2000 ; Waldeyer et al., 2022 ). These associations are particularly relevant in GenAI-supported learning because external assistance is readily available when academic work becomes difficult. Under such conditions, students’ capacity to sustain their own effort remains an important learner-controlled component of the learning process. The significant negative indirect association further indicates that GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes were statistically connected through effort regulation within the specified model. This association should be interpreted in light of the measures’ reference frames: GenAI dependency was specific to reliance on generative AI, whereas effort regulation reflected a broader academic self-regulatory tendency and perceived learning outcomes referred to recent coursework rather than a specific GenAI-supported task. The comparison of unadjusted and frequency-adjusted score-based models provided a more differentiated assessment of robustness. The negative association between GenAI dependency and effort regulation, the positive association between effort regulation and perceived learning outcomes, and the negative indirect association remained similar after adjustment for GenAI use frequency. However, the small negative total association was no longer statistically significant in the adjusted model, indicating that the evidence for this overall relationship was less robust. The change in the total coefficient was small and should not be interpreted as demonstrating that use frequency substantially explained the association. These results suggest that dependency-oriented reliance and frequency of GenAI use should be distinguished, but they do not establish their independent causal contributions to learning. Because the data were cross-sectional, the indirect association represents a statistical feature of the specified model rather than evidence of a causal mechanism. Reverse, reciprocal, and alternative directional relationships remain plausible. Moreover, the score-based sensitivity estimates should not be directly compared with the coefficients from the primary latent-variable SEM because the two approaches differ in their measurement specifications. The findings contribute to self-regulated learning research by identifying effort regulation as a specific resource-management process associated with dependency-oriented GenAI use and perceived learning outcomes. The negative indirect association suggests that learner-controlled persistence is relevant when examining students’ reliance on readily available AI assistance. However, GenAI dependency explained only 6.6% of the variance in effort regulation, indicating that other motivational, instructional, and contextual factors remain important. The distinction between dependency and frequency of use further suggests that frequent GenAI engagement should not automatically be interpreted as problematic reliance. Because perceived learning outcomes reflected students’ broader evaluations of recent coursework, these findings extend understanding of subjective learning experiences without establishing effects on task-specific or objectively assessed performance.
